title: The technician decline is not what it seems
html:
The dental technician register is in decline, but Matt Everatt explains why the figures do not tell the whole story and where the true danger lies.

In August 2021, I wrote about the declining numbers of dental technicians. The article headline was intentionally blunt: ‘By 2040, dental technicians will be extinct.’ Although it is very unlikely to go that far, it was based on the trajectory of the numbers, and I wrote it to sensationalise the message.

The figures were stark. In 2018, 6,163 dental technicians were registered with the General Dental Council (GDC). By 2021, that had fallen to 5,535. By 2026, we are now below 5,000 for the first time. There were just 143 new registrations last year in the entire UK.

The decline is real, but the story behind those numbers is more complicated and perhaps not as grim as they may first seem.

What the technology actually changed

CAD/CAM, 3D printing, digital design, and automation have fundamentally changed what technicians can produce. An experienced technician using modern workflows can deliver work that once required several varied skills often from different technicians. Accuracy is better, reproducibility is reliable and the quality has arguably risen.

This is progress, not a problem. It means the profession genuinely does not need as many registered technicians as it did in 2018. Some decline is inevitable. Some is healthy, but not all of what we are seeing is inevitable.

Inevitable versus chosen decline

If technology efficiency was the only factor, the register would fall to a lower sustainable level. Fewer technicians, more highly skilled, paid better, using advanced technology for premium work. That is a viable profession.

That is not happening. Technology-driven efficiency is colliding with structural choices that are unsustainable. We use efficiency gains to cut prices instead of improving margins. Unregulated manufacturers are still going unchecked, along with chairside manufacturing, distorting the market. We also do a pretty good job of making the profession unattractive to younger or newcomers, so fewer people join. These are choices and they compound the inevitable decline into something far worse.

Two paths forward

We can continue as we are, compete on price, accept unregulated competition, pay people as little as possible, watch training institutions close. In ten years, 3,000 technicians, most over 50, many exhausted. The profession continues its demise towards obsolescence.

Or we accept technology-driven efficiency as the new way and make different structural choices. Stop undercutting. Price on value and expertise. Address unregulated manufacturing. Use margins to pay technicians better and create real development pathways. Run labs as proper businesses. In ten years, 3,500 registered technicians, well-paid, highly skilled, specialised in complex work. A smaller profession that is thriving.

Both futures are possible. Neither is inevitable. The choice is mostly ours.

If we want a profession to exist

If we choose to be the thriving profession rather than the diminished one, we need to stop competing on price. Not because it feels good, but because it is the only way margins improve enough to pay people well and invest in quality. Some clients will leave. Let them. The ones attracted by price are the ones most likely to be demanding, slow to pay, and quick to complain. They are not worth keeping.

We need to invest those margins in people. Pay laboratory technicians what they are worth, salaries that reflect their expertise and regulated status. Invest in development and specialisation. When you do this, good technicians stay.

Quality improves, reputation compounds and the phone rings more often than you could imagine.

We need to collectively address unregulated manufacturing. The GDC and MHRA have regulations. They need to be enforced. As a collective, we can do more to make our voices heard. Dental practices need to understand that work produced outside regulatory frameworks carries real liability. This is not negotiable if we want standards to mean anything.

We need training institutions properly resourced. You cannot sustain viable programmes on cohorts of a dozen students with shoestring budgets. If the profession wants technicians capable of advanced work, education has to be funded accordingly. There are good moves towards supporting apprenticeships. Labs need to be onboard to support these institutions.
